groups.name: Cycadophyta
groups.fact: Palm-like seed plants with stout trunks and pinnate leaves, and among the few seed plants still producing motile sperm.

groups.name: Ginkgophyta
groups.fact: A seed-plant lineage reduced to one living species, with fan-shaped, dichotomously veined leaves.

groups.name: Pinaceae
groups.fact: The pine family: resinous conifers with needle leaves, woody seed cones and, in most genera, needles borne in bundles.

groups.name: Magnoliids
groups.fact: Flowering plants outside both the monocots and the eudicots, with pollen of a single aperture; the group includes the laurels, magnolias and peppers.

groups.name: Laurales
groups.fact: Mostly aromatic woody magnoliids with small flowers and a cup-shaped floral receptacle.

groups.name: Lauraceae
groups.fact: Aromatic evergreen trees and shrubs whose bark, leaf and fruit carry essential oils; the family gives cinnamon, bay, camphor and avocado.

groups.name: Magnoliales
groups.fact: Woody magnoliids with large flowers of many free parts, pollinated by beetles in the most ancient families.

groups.name: Magnoliaceae
groups.fact: Trees and shrubs whose flower parts spiral up a single elongated axis rather than sitting in whorls.

groups.name: Myristicaceae
groups.fact: Tropical trees with red sap and a seed wrapped in a lacy aril; nutmeg and mace come from one species.

groups.name: Annonaceae
groups.fact: The custard-apple family: tropical trees with fleshy aggregate fruits and flowers in threes.

groups.name: Piperales
groups.fact: Magnoliids with swollen stem nodes and tiny flowers packed onto a spike.

groups.name: Piperaceae
groups.fact: Pepper vines and their relatives: minute flowers on a dense spike, ripening into single-seeded drupes.

groups.name: Austrobaileyales
groups.fact: One of the earliest-branching lineages of flowering plants, sitting outside the magnoliids, monocots and eudicots alike.

groups.name: Schisandraceae
groups.fact: Aromatic woody plants whose carpels ripen separately and spread into a star or a head of berries.

groups.name: Poales
groups.fact: The largest monocot order: grasses, sedges, rushes and bromeliads, most of them wind-pollinated with reduced flowers.

groups.name: Poaceae
groups.fact: The grass family: hollow jointed stems, leaves in two ranks with a sheath around the stem, and growth from the base rather than the tip, which is why grazing does not kill them.

groups.name: Bromeliaceae
groups.fact: Mostly New World monocots with leaves in a water-holding rosette and absorptive scales on the leaf surface.

groups.name: Cyperaceae
groups.fact: Sedges: solid, usually triangular stems and leaves in three ranks, unlike a grass's round hollow stem and two ranks.

groups.name: Typhaceae
groups.fact: Marsh monocots whose minute flowers pack into a dense cylindrical spike above narrow strap leaves.

groups.name: Zingiberales
groups.fact: Large-leaved tropical monocots with strongly asymmetric flowers, including bananas, gingers and their relatives.

groups.name: Zingiberaceae
groups.fact: The ginger family: aromatic perennials growing from fleshy rhizomes, with one fertile stamen and showy petal-like staminodes.

groups.name: Musaceae
groups.fact: Giant herbs whose overlapping leaf sheaths form a false trunk; the true stem only emerges to flower.

groups.name: Dioscoreales
groups.fact: Monocots with net-veined leaves — unusual in the group — and often a starchy underground tuber.

groups.name: Dioscoreaceae
groups.fact: Twining vines storing starch in tubers; the family is the source of the diosgenin used to synthesise steroid hormones.

groups.name: Amaryllidaceae
groups.fact: Bulbous monocots with flowers in an umbel; the onion subfamily makes sulfur compounds released only when the tissue is cut.

groups.name: Iridaceae
groups.fact: Monocots with equitant, flattened leaves and flowers of three stamens and an inferior ovary.

groups.name: Asphodelaceae
groups.fact: Monocots including the aloes, with succulent leaves holding a mucilaginous gel and a bitter sap just beneath the rind.

groups.name: Proteales
groups.fact: An early-branching eudicot order of very mixed appearance, from plane trees and proteas to the sacred lotus.

groups.name: Nelumbonaceae
groups.fact: Aquatic plants rooted in mud, with peltate leaves held clear of the water and seeds embedded in a flat-topped receptacle.

groups.name: Proteaceae
groups.fact: Mostly Southern Hemisphere woody plants with clustered proteoid roots that mine phosphorus from poor soils.

groups.name: Brassicales
groups.fact: Eudicots that make glucosinolates — mustard oil glycosides released as pungent isothiocyanates the moment the tissue is damaged.

groups.name: Brassicaceae
groups.fact: The mustard family: four petals in a cross, six stamens with two short, and a two-chambered fruit that splits leaving a papery partition.

groups.name: Capparaceae
groups.fact: Shrubs and small trees of dry country with long-stamened flowers and berry-like fruit.

groups.name: Caricaceae
groups.fact: Soft-stemmed tropical plants with milky latex rich in the protein-digesting enzyme papain.

groups.name: Tropaeolaceae
groups.fact: New World herbs with peltate leaves and spurred flowers; the whole plant is peppery from its glucosinolates.

groups.name: Malvales
groups.fact: Eudicots with mucilage canals, tough fibrous inner bark and, typically, stellate hairs.

groups.name: Malvaceae
groups.fact: The mallow family: stamens fused into a tube around the style, and a fibrous bast in the inner bark; it holds cotton, cocoa, okra, baobab and linden.

groups.name: Thymelaeaceae
groups.fact: Woody plants with exceptionally tough bark fibre and no petals, the calyx doing the flower's advertising.

groups.name: Bixaceae
groups.fact: Tropical shrubs and small trees whose seeds carry a waxy carotenoid coat used as a dye.

groups.name: Vitales
groups.fact: A single-family eudicot order of climbing plants that grip with tendrils opposite the leaves.

groups.name: Vitaceae
groups.fact: The grape family: climbers with leaf-opposed tendrils, swollen stem nodes and berries with a small number of hard seeds.

groups.name: Myrtales
groups.fact: Eudicots with opposite leaves, internal phloem inside the xylem ring, and flower parts set on a cup-shaped hypanthium.

groups.name: Myrtaceae
groups.fact: Aromatic evergreens whose leaves are dotted with oil glands visible against the light, and whose flowers are mostly stamens.

groups.name: Lythraceae
groups.fact: Herbs, shrubs and trees with flower parts set on a tubular hypanthium; the family includes the pomegranate.

groups.name: Fagales
groups.fact: Wind-pollinated woody eudicots bearing catkins, and fruiting in a hard one-seeded nut.

groups.name: Fagaceae
groups.fact: The beech family: a nut sitting in or under a scaly or spiny cupule, and tannin-rich wood and bark.

groups.name: Betulaceae
groups.fact: The birch family: doubly-toothed leaves, male catkins formed the previous season, and small winged or husked nuts.

groups.name: Juglandaceae
groups.fact: Aromatic pinnate-leaved trees whose fruit is a nut inside a husk that is not part of the fruit wall.

groups.name: Myricaceae
groups.fact: Aromatic shrubs with resin-dotted leaves, most fixing nitrogen through root nodules of Frankia.

groups.name: Cucurbitales
groups.fact: Eudicots with mostly unisexual flowers and an inferior ovary, including the gourds and the begonias.

groups.name: Cucurbitaceae
groups.fact: The gourd family: tendril-bearing vines with separate male and female flowers, fruiting in a pepo — a berry with a hard rind.

groups.name: Saxifragales
groups.fact: A morphologically scattered eudicot order held together by molecular data, from stonecrops to currants and witch hazel.

groups.name: Grossulariaceae
groups.fact: Shrubs of the genus Ribes, bearing berries tipped with the withered remains of the flower.

groups.name: Dipsacales
groups.fact: Eudicots with opposite leaves and small flowers packed into dense heads or flat-topped clusters.

groups.name: Adoxaceae
groups.fact: Shrubs and small trees with compound or lobed opposite leaves and flat clusters of small flowers ripening into drupes.

groups.name: Aquifoliales
groups.fact: Eudicots with small four-parted flowers, usually on separate male and female plants, ripening into a berry-like drupe.

groups.name: Aquifoliaceae
groups.fact: The hollies: a single genus of evergreen or deciduous woody plants, dioecious, with drupes of several one-seeded stones.

groups.name: Boraginales
groups.fact: Eudicots with bristly hairs and flowers arranged along a one-sided coiled cyme that unrolls as it opens.

groups.name: Boraginaceae
groups.fact: Rough-haired plants whose fruit splits into four one-seeded nutlets.

groups.name: Amaranthaceae
groups.fact: Includes the old goosefoot family: salt- and drought-tolerant plants with tiny wind-pollinated flowers, many of them C4.

groups.name: Polygonaceae
groups.fact: The knotweed family: swollen stem nodes sheathed in a papery ochrea, and a three-angled one-seeded fruit.

groups.name: Basellaceae
groups.fact: Succulent twining vines with mucilaginous leaves and small flowers that often never fully open.

groups.name: Aizoaceae
groups.fact: Mostly southern African succulents with bladder cells on the leaf surface that store water and salt.

groups.name: Simmondsiaceae
groups.fact: A single desert shrub genus whose seed stores liquid wax esters rather than the triglyceride oil every other seed plant uses.

groups.name: Rosaceae
groups.fact: The rose family: five-petalled flowers on a hypanthium, leaves with stipules, and fruit as varied as a pome, a drupe and an aggregate of drupelets.

groups.name: Moraceae
groups.fact: The mulberry and fig family: milky latex, and tiny flowers packed into or onto a fleshy common receptacle.

groups.name: Ulmaceae
groups.fact: Trees with asymmetric leaf bases and doubly-toothed margins, fruiting in a flat winged samara.

groups.name: Rhamnaceae
groups.fact: The buckthorn family: often thorny woody plants with small greenish flowers and a fleshy drupe.

groups.name: Urticaceae
groups.fact: The nettle family: opposite or alternate leaves with cystoliths, and long, exceptionally strong bast fibres in the stem.

groups.name: Elaeagnaceae
groups.fact: Shrubs covered in silvery peltate scales, fixing nitrogen through root nodules of Frankia.

groups.name: Rutaceae
groups.fact: The citrus family: leaves dotted with translucent oil glands, and in the citrus genus a fruit called a hesperidium — a leathery oil-rich rind over juice-filled vesicles.

groups.name: Anacardiaceae
groups.fact: Resinous trees and shrubs; many carry alkyl catechols such as urushiol that cause contact dermatitis.

groups.name: Meliaceae
groups.fact: The mahogany family: pinnate-leaved tropical trees with stamens fused into a tube and durable, often fragrant timber.

groups.name: Burseraceae
groups.fact: Trees whose bark carries resin canals; cut, they bleed an aromatic oleo-gum-resin that hardens in air.

groups.name: Simaroubaceae
groups.fact: Woody plants whose bark and wood carry intensely bitter quassinoid triterpenes.

groups.name: Theaceae
groups.fact: Evergreen woody plants with alternate toothed leaves and showy flowers of many stamens; the family includes the tea plant.

groups.name: Actinidiaceae
groups.fact: Woody climbers, mostly with separate male and female plants, fruiting in a many-seeded berry.

groups.name: Ebenaceae
groups.fact: Trees with very dark, dense heartwood and usually separate male and female plants.

groups.name: Sapotaceae
groups.fact: Tropical trees with milky latex and seeds rich in solid fats.

groups.name: Lecythidaceae
groups.fact: Tropical trees whose woody fruit opens by a lid, releasing large angular seeds.

groups.name: Rubiaceae
groups.fact: The coffee family: opposite leaves joined by stipules between them, an inferior ovary, and alkaloid-rich bark and seed.

groups.name: Oleaceae
groups.fact: The olive family: opposite leaves, flowers with only two stamens, and fruit ranging from a drupe to a winged samara.

groups.name: Pedaliaceae
groups.fact: Mostly African and Asian herbs with mucilage glands, fruiting in a capsule that splits when the seed is ripe.

groups.name: Plantaginaceae
groups.fact: A large lamialean family holding plantains, snapdragons and foxgloves; several genera make cardiac glycosides.

groups.name: Araliaceae
groups.fact: The ivy family: woody and herbaceous plants with flowers in umbels, sister to the carrot family.

groups.name: Salicaceae
groups.fact: The willow family: separate male and female catkins, tiny seeds carried on cottony hairs, and bark rich in salicylates.

groups.name: Linaceae
groups.fact: Slender herbs whose stems carry long bast fibres, and whose seeds are rich in drying oil.

groups.name: Passifloraceae
groups.fact: Tendril-climbing plants whose flowers carry a corona of filaments between petals and stamens.

groups.name: Clusiaceae
groups.fact: Tropical woody plants with opposite leaves and yellow or clear resinous latex.

groups.name: Phyllanthaceae
groups.fact: Split from the spurge family and unlike it in having no milky latex; leaves are often arranged so a branchlet mimics a compound leaf.

groups.name: Rhizophoraceae
groups.fact: Mostly tropical coastal trees; the mangrove genera prop themselves on arching stilt roots and germinate the seed while it still hangs on the parent.

groups.name: Tetrapoda
groups.fact: Vertebrates descended from lobe-finned fish with four limbs built on the same one-bone, two-bone, digits plan — a group that still includes limbless snakes and caecilians.

groups.name: Amniota
groups.fact: Tetrapods whose embryo develops inside its own fluid-filled amnion, so the egg no longer has to be laid in water.

groups.name: Synapsida
groups.fact: Amniotes with a single temporal opening behind each eye socket for the jaw muscle — the branch that leads to every mammal.

groups.name: Therapsida
groups.fact: Synapsids with teeth differentiated into incisors, canines and postcanines, and limbs held under the body rather than sprawled.

groups.name: Cynodontia
groups.fact: Therapsids named for their dog-like canines; the group includes the direct ancestors of mammals.

groups.name: Sauropsida
groups.fact: The amniote branch holding every reptile and bird; it excretes nitrogen as insoluble uric acid rather than urea.

groups.name: Marsupialia
groups.fact: Mammals with a very short gestation and no full placenta, so the young finishes development attached to a teat, usually inside a pouch.

groups.name: Placentalia
groups.fact: Mammals whose fetus is nourished through a chorioallantoic placenta for a long gestation, the two bloodstreams never mixing.

groups.name: Multituberculata
groups.fact: Extinct rodent-like mammals named for the rows of cusps on their molars; they ran for over 130 million years, longer than any other mammal lineage.

groups.name: Chiroptera
groups.fact: The only mammals capable of true powered flight, on a membrane stretched between four enormously elongated fingers.

groups.name: Phyllostomidae
groups.fact: New World leaf-nosed bats, the most dietarily varied bat family — fruit, nectar, insects, frogs and, in three species, blood.

groups.name: Sirenia
groups.fact: Fully aquatic herbivorous mammals with paddle forelimbs, no hind limbs and dense pachyostotic bones for ballast.

groups.name: Hyracoidea
groups.fact: Small, stout herbivores with rubbery foot pads and continuously growing tusk-like incisors; their nearest relatives are elephants and sirenians.

groups.name: Macroscelidea
groups.fact: Sengis, or elephant shrews: long-snouted African insectivores that are afrotherians, not shrews.

groups.name: Afrosoricida
groups.fact: African afrotherian insectivores — the tenrecs and the golden moles — convergent on hedgehogs, shrews and moles but unrelated to them.

groups.name: Tubulidentata
groups.fact: Named for teeth built of many parallel dentine tubes with no enamel; a single living species digs termite mounds in Africa.

groups.name: Pholidota
groups.fact: The only mammals armoured in true keratin scales; toothless, with a long sticky tongue anchored near the pelvis.

groups.name: Dermoptera
groups.fact: Colugos: gliding mammals with the most extensive skin membrane of any mammal, running from neck to fingertips to tail.

groups.name: Didelphimorphia
groups.fact: American opossums, the oldest surviving marsupial order in the New World.

groups.name: Dasyuromorphia
groups.fact: Australasian carnivorous marsupials, from the numbat and dunnarts to the Tasmanian devil.

groups.name: Tachyglossidae
groups.fact: Echidnas: spiny egg-laying mammals that incubate a single leathery egg in a temporary pouch.

groups.name: Talpidae
groups.fact: Moles and their kin: cylindrical burrowers with outward-facing spade forelimbs and a huge humerus for digging leverage.

groups.name: Solenodontidae
groups.fact: Caribbean insectivores, and among the very few venomous mammals — venom runs down grooves in the second lower incisors.

groups.name: Elephantidae
groups.fact: Proboscideans with tusks from the upper incisors and molars that erupt in sequence from the back, each replacing the last as it wears out.

groups.name: Hippopotamidae
groups.fact: Barrel-bodied semi-aquatic artiodactyls with a three-chambered non-ruminating stomach; their closest living relatives are the whales.

groups.name: Giraffidae
groups.fact: Ruminants bearing ossicones — bone cores under skin, present at birth and fused to the skull only at maturity.

groups.name: Antilocapridae
groups.fact: North American ruminants with branched horns whose keratin sheath is shed and regrown each year, a combination no other animal has.

groups.name: Camelidae
groups.fact: Ruminant-like artiodactyls with a three-chambered stomach, padded two-toed feet and oval red blood cells.

groups.name: Suidae
groups.fact: Non-ruminating omnivorous artiodactyls with a simple stomach, a mobile cartilaginous snout disc and ever-growing canine tusks.

groups.name: Bovidae
groups.fact: Ruminants with unbranched horns of a permanent keratin sheath over a bone core, never shed.

groups.name: Equidae
groups.fact: Odd-toed ungulates reduced to a single weight-bearing third toe capped in a hoof, and fermenting plants in an enlarged caecum.

groups.name: Equus
groups.fact: The only surviving horse genus — horses, asses and zebras. It arose in North America about 4 million years ago and died out there about 12,000 years ago.

groups.name: Tapiridae
groups.fact: Perissodactyls with a short prehensile proboscis of fused nose and upper lip, four toes in front and three behind.

groups.name: Dicerorhinus
groups.fact: The Sumatran rhinoceros: the smallest living rhino, the only Asian one with two horns, and the only one with a coat of hair.

groups.name: Vombatidae
groups.fact: Burrowing marsupials with a backward-facing pouch and continuously growing rootless teeth.

groups.name: Burramyidae
groups.fact: Pygmy possums: tiny Australian marsupials, and the only small Australian mammals that truly hibernate.

groups.name: Phocoenidae
groups.fact: Porpoises: small toothed whales with flat spade-shaped teeth and no pronounced beak.

groups.name: Lipotidae
groups.fact: The Yangtze river dolphin and its fossil kin — a freshwater cetacean lineage now believed extinct.

groups.name: Homo
groups.fact: The hominin genus defined by an enlarged brain, reduced chewing teeth and habitual stone tool use; only one species survives.

groups.name: Australopithecus
groups.fact: African hominins that walked upright on essentially modern lower limbs while keeping an ape-sized brain and long arms.

groups.name: Paranthropus
groups.fact: Robust hominins with huge molars, flaring cheekbones and a sagittal crest anchoring the chewing muscle — an extinct side branch.

groups.name: Ardipithecus
groups.fact: Early Ethiopian hominins that walked upright yet still had a grasping, divergent big toe for climbing.

groups.name: Sahelanthropus
groups.fact: A roughly 7-million-year-old Chadian hominin known from one distorted skull; whether it walked upright is still disputed.

groups.name: Orrorin
groups.fact: A 6-million-year-old Kenyan hominin known mainly from femora whose neck shape suggests upright walking.

groups.name: Passeriformes
groups.fact: Perching birds: three toes forward and one strongly backward, with a tendon arrangement that grips as the leg bends. More than half of all bird species.

groups.name: Thraupidae
groups.fact: Tanagers: a large New World songbird family whose beak shape tracks diet closely, and which includes Darwin's finches.

groups.name: Ptilonorhynchidae
groups.fact: Bowerbirds: Australasian songbirds whose males build and decorate a display bower that is not a nest.

groups.name: Apodiformes
groups.fact: Birds with very short humeri and long hand bones, giving a wing driven almost entirely from the shoulder — swifts and hummingbirds.

groups.name: Apodidae
groups.fact: Swifts: legs too short for walking, so they feed, mate and sleep on the wing and cling rather than perch.

groups.name: Trochilidae
groups.fact: Hummingbirds: a shoulder joint that rotates the whole wing, so the wing generates lift on the upstroke as well as the down.

groups.name: Sphenisciformes
groups.fact: Penguins: flightless seabirds whose wings became stiff flippers and whose bones are solid rather than air-filled.

groups.name: Phoenicopteriformes
groups.fact: Flamingos: long-legged filter feeders whose bent bill is worked upside down, lamellae straining food from the water.

groups.name: Procellariiformes
groups.fact: Tubenoses: seabirds with tubular nostrils, a salt gland above the eye, and a strong sense of smell.

groups.name: Diomedeidae
groups.fact: Albatrosses: a shoulder-lock tendon holds the wing open so the bird glides on wind for hours without muscular effort.

groups.name: Struthioniformes
groups.fact: Ostriches: flightless ratites with no keel on the sternum and, uniquely among birds, only two toes on each foot.

groups.name: Apterygiformes
groups.fact: Kiwi: flightless New Zealand ratites, the only birds with nostrils at the tip of the bill.

groups.name: Piciformes
groups.fact: Mostly zygodactyl arboreal birds — two toes forward, two back — nesting in cavities, including woodpeckers and toucans.

groups.name: Picidae
groups.fact: Woodpeckers: a stiff tail for bracing, a chisel bill, and a hyoid apparatus that wraps around the skull.

groups.name: Ramphastidae
groups.fact: Toucans: an enormous hollow bill of keratin over a bony strut lattice, used to reach fruit and to shed heat.

groups.name: Pelecaniformes
groups.fact: Mostly waterbirds with a bare throat patch and, in many families, a dagger bill and a folding S-shaped neck.

groups.name: Pelecanidae
groups.fact: Pelicans: an expandable throat pouch used as a dip net, drained of water before the fish is swallowed.

groups.name: Ardeidae
groups.fact: Herons and bitterns: modified neck vertebrae fold into a tight S so the bill can be shot forward to strike.

groups.name: Threskiornithidae
groups.fact: Ibises and spoonbills: wading birds probing mud with a long decurved or spatulate bill.

groups.name: Suliformes
groups.fact: Plunge-diving and pursuit-diving seabirds — gannets, cormorants, frigatebirds and darters — with all four toes webbed.

groups.name: Phalacrocoracidae
groups.fact: Cormorants: pursuit divers with wettable outer plumage that reduces buoyancy, hence the wing-spread drying posture.

groups.name: Psittaciformes
groups.fact: Parrots: a strongly hooked bill whose upper mandible hinges on the skull rather than fusing to it, and zygodactyl feet used like hands.

groups.name: Columbiformes
groups.fact: Pigeons and doves: they drink by suction without lifting the head, and feed their young on crop milk.

groups.name: Columbidae
groups.fact: Stout-bodied short-necked birds with a fleshy cere at the bill base; both parents secrete crop milk.

groups.name: Tytonidae
groups.fact: Barn owls: a heart-shaped facial disc and vertically offset ear openings that let them locate prey by sound alone.

groups.name: Mesitornithiformes
groups.fact: Mesites: three weak-flying ground-foraging bird species found only in Madagascar.

groups.name: Eurypygiformes
groups.fact: A two-species order — the kagu of New Caledonia and the sunbittern of the Neotropics — sister taxa despite living oceans apart.

groups.name: Musophagiformes
groups.fact: Turacos: African birds carrying true green and red feather pigments, turacoverdin and turacin, which almost no other bird makes.

groups.name: Opisthocomiformes
groups.fact: The hoatzin alone: a leaf-eater that ferments its food in an enlarged crop, and whose chicks bear claws on the wing.

groups.name: Cariamiformes
groups.fact: Seriemas and their extinct kin, including the terror birds; living species kill prey by beating it against the ground.

groups.name: Leptosomiformes
groups.fact: The cuckoo-roller of Madagascar and the Comoros, sole member of its own order and no relative of cuckoos or rollers.

groups.name: Rhynchocephalia
groups.fact: A reptile order reduced to the tuatara alone, with a diapsid skull keeping both temporal arches and a parietal third eye in the hatchling.

groups.name: Ichthyosauria
groups.fact: Extinct marine reptiles convergent on dolphins, with a fish-like tail fin and enormous sclerotic eye rings; they bore live young at sea.

groups.name: Dermochelyidae
groups.fact: The leatherback: a sea turtle with no bony shell plates, a leathery skin over a mosaic of dermal ossicles, and countercurrent heat exchange that holds its core well above sea temperature.

groups.name: Amphisbaenia
groups.fact: Worm lizards: limbless burrowing squamates with annulated skin and a heavily reinforced skull used as a digging tool.

groups.name: Naja
groups.fact: True cobras: elapids that rear and spread a hood of extended cervical ribs when threatened.

groups.name: Bufo
groups.fact: True toads: warty dry skin, paired parotoid glands behind the eyes, and a walking rather than hopping gait.

groups.name: Cryptobranchidae
groups.fact: Giant salamanders: fully aquatic, lungless in effect, breathing through heavily wrinkled skin that multiplies their surface area.

groups.name: Pipidae
groups.fact: Tongueless aquatic frogs of Africa and South America, with a lateral line retained into adulthood.

groups.name: Myxini
groups.fact: Hagfish: jawless craniates with a skull but no vertebral column, and slime glands that gel seawater in an instant.

groups.name: Placodermi
groups.fact: Extinct armoured fish, among the first jawed vertebrates, with head and thorax encased in bony plates joined at a neck hinge.

groups.name: Acanthodii
groups.fact: The 'spiny sharks': extinct fish with a stout spine in front of nearly every fin, now understood as a stem group of the cartilaginous fish.

groups.name: Sarcopterygii
groups.fact: Lobe-finned fish: paired fins borne on a fleshy stalk with internal limb bones, the lineage from which every tetrapod descends.

groups.name: Dipnoi
groups.fact: Lungfish: sarcopterygians that retain functional lungs and can breathe air when their water runs short of oxygen.

groups.name: Actinistia
groups.fact: Coelacanths: lobe-finned fish with a hollow notochord retained in the adult and an intracranial joint splitting the braincase.

groups.name: Gymnotiformes
groups.fact: South American knifefish: they swim by undulating a long anal fin and navigate by generating their own electric field.

groups.name: Myctophiformes
groups.fact: Lanternfish: small deep-sea fish patterned with light organs, and among the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.

groups.name: Stomiiformes
groups.fact: Deep-sea fish with rows of ventral photophores used for counter-illumination against the faint light from above.

groups.name: Scombriformes
groups.fact: Fast open-water fish with a streamlined body, finlets behind the dorsal and anal fins, and a narrow keeled tail base.

groups.name: Thecostraca
groups.fact: Crustaceans including the barnacles: they settle head-first, cement themselves down and filter with feathery modified legs.

groups.name: Indriidae
groups.fact: The largest living lemurs — indri, sifakas and woolly lemurs — all of them leapers that hold the trunk upright.

groups.name: Phascolarctidae
groups.fact: The koala and its fossil relatives; the wombats are the other surviving branch of the same suborder.

groups.name: Onychophora
groups.fact: Velvet worms: a phylum of their own, sister to the arthropods, walking on stubby unjointed legs and firing glue at prey.

groups.name: Heterodontosauridae
groups.fact: Small early ornithischians with three kinds of tooth in one jaw, which is what the name says.

groups.name: Lycoperdon
groups.fact: The puffballs — same family as the button mushroom, but they ripen into a dry sac and puff their spores out through a pore.

groups.name: Chelicerata
groups.fact: Arthropods whose first pair of appendages are chelicerae — pincers or fangs in front of the mouth — and which have no antennae at all.

groups.name: Crustacea
groups.fact: Arthropods with two pairs of antennae, a hardened exoskeleton usually stiffened with calcium carbonate, and limbs that branch in two.

groups.name: Pycnogonida
groups.fact: Sea spiders: chelicerates with a body so reduced that most of the gut and the gonads run out into the legs.

groups.name: Xiphosura
groups.fact: Horseshoe crabs, chelicerates rather than crabs, with a hinged horseshoe carapace and a spike-like tail used to right themselves.
